etymology: From Greek aura (breeze, breath), long used for an intangible atmosphere around a person; revived c. 2024 by Gen-Z and Gen Alpha as a points-economy of coolness — effortless composure earns "aura," embarrassment means "losing aura points."
biblical_def: In current youth slang, aura is the invisible currency of cool: an intangible presence or gravitas a person carries. Doing something impressive without trying "gains aura"; tripping in the hallway is "minus 1,000 aura points." The joke-economy is half-ironic, but the value system underneath is dead serious: the highest good is effortless self-possession admired by others, and life is scored by how one appears. The Christian observation: Scripture knows the reality this word grasps at — there IS such a thing as weight in a person. Moses' face shone when he had been with God (Exo 34:29); the council "took knowledge" of unschooled apostles, "that they had been with Jesus" (Acts 4:13); the Proverbs speak of a man's spirit being known. But biblical gravitas is the byproduct of communion with God and character formed by Him — never a score to farm, never self-generated, and never for self-glory. A generation taught to husband its own mystique is being discipled into self-worship by points. Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth (Prov 27:2); and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? (1 Cor 4:7).
webster_summary: Gen-Z/Gen Alpha points-economy of intangible cool (c. 2024): impressive composure "gains aura," embarrassment "loses aura points"; the real thing it gropes for — weight of presence — comes only from God.
webster_full: AURA, n. (Gen-Z / Gen Alpha slang, c. 2024–present) The intangible currency of coolness; impressive or composed behavior "gains aura," embarrassing moments "lose aura points."
Often used numerically and half-ironically: "minus 1,000 aura" for a public stumble.
Derivative: aura farming — deliberately performing composure to accumulate perceived coolness.
The older English sense (an atmosphere surrounding a person) and the occult sense (an energy field) both predate the slang; the slang borrows the mystique without the metaphysics.
Decode for parents: your teen is describing social gravitas as a video-game score.
scriptures: Prov 27:2
Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips.
1 Cor 4:7
For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?
...Moses wist not that the skin of his face shone while he talked with him.
Acts 4:13
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.
corruption_summary: Aura-culture trains the young to treat self-presentation as a scored economy — presence cultivated for self-glory — when true weight of character is the unsought byproduct of being with God.
corruption_paragraphs: The points-economy of self. "Aura points" make a game of what the heart already wanted: to be admired without appearing to seek it. That is vainglory with better branding — the cultivated mystique of a self curated for spectators. Scripture's verdict on self-husbanded glory is constant: let another praise thee, and not thine own mouth; he that exalteth himself shall be abased. The Christian does not farm presence; he forgets himself in the presence of God.

The real thing exists. The slang testifies, despite itself, that some people carry weight that cannot be explained by looks or volume. The Bible shows its true source: Moses' face shone and he wist not; the apostles' boldness was traced to having been with Jesus. Gravitas is communion-residue — given, not farmed; noticed by others, unnoticed by its bearer. Tell a young man chasing aura: spend it on the face of God, and you will come down the mountain shining without knowing it.
roots_summary: Greek aura (breath, breeze) → English "intangible atmosphere around a person" → Gen-Z points-economy of cool (c. 2024): composure gains it, embarrassment loses it.
roots_lines: Greek aura — breath, breeze; later, an intangible emanation or atmosphere
19th-20th c. English: the felt presence or atmosphere surrounding a person
Occult/New Age use: a personal energy field (not the slang sense)
c. 2024 Gen-Z / Gen Alpha: a scored economy of effortless cool ("aura points")
Derivative: aura farming — performing composure to harvest admiration
usage: "Bro caught the ball one-handed and didn't even look — infinite aura."
The slang scores what Scripture sources: presence is real, but it is communion-residue, not a stat.
Aura farming is vainglory with a gamer's vocabulary; Moses' shining face was the real thing, unsought.

etymology: From the 2024-25 viral spread of the rap song Doot Doot (6 7) by Skrilla through basketball edits and classroom meme culture; shouted by kids with a two-handed juggling gesture. It means, by the users' own cheerful admission, essentially nothing.
biblical_def: Six seven is the purest specimen yet of meaning-free youth slang: a number pair from a rap hook, shouted with a palms-up juggling gesture, whose entire function is the in-group laugh of recognition. Asked what it means, kids answer — delightedly — that it doesn't mean anything; saying it IS the joke. Teachers report whole classrooms erupting when any combination of six and seven occurs in a math problem. It was even named a 2025 word of the year, precisely for its meaninglessness. The Christian observation runs along two tracks. First, fair-mindedness: nonsense play is not new (every generation had its noise), children's wordplay is not sin, and a father who can laugh at it earns the standing to talk about it. Second, the sober track: a dialect WHOLLY built of severed words trains the soul to treat language — God's appointed carrier of truth, promise, and confession — as disposable noise. The Lord's warning stands over every age's chatter: every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment (Matt 12:36). The fitting response is neither panic nor surrender: play with your kids, and then feed them words with weight.
webster_summary: Gen Alpha's flagship nonsense interjection (c. 2024-25), from Skrilla's Doot Doot (6 7): shouted with a juggling gesture, meaning — proudly — nothing; an occasion to teach the weight of words without despising play.
webster_full: SIX SEVEN (6-7), interj. (Gen Alpha / Gen-Z slang, c. 2024–present) A deliberately meaningless catchphrase from the rap song Doot Doot (6 7), spread through basketball edits and school meme culture.
Performed with a two-handed, palms-up juggling gesture.
Triggered by any incidental occurrence of the numbers six and seven (page numbers, math problems, jersey numbers).
Its admitted meaninglessness is the point: an in-group recognition signal, not a statement.
Decode for parents: it is not code for anything; it is the laugh of belonging. Laugh once, then teach words that mean things.
scriptures: Matt 12:36
But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
Eph 5:4
Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks.
Prov 25:11
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
Eccl 3:4
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
corruption_summary: Not corruption of a good word but the manufacture of wordless words: a dialect of severed signifiers that, as a steady diet, trains the young to handle language — and therefore truth — lightly.
corruption_paragraphs: The brainrot economy. Six-seven did not arise organically from the playground; it was farmed by an attention economy that profits when repetition replaces meaning. Each cycle of these severed words is shorter and emptier than the last — skibidi to six-seven inside two years — because the algorithm rewards the laugh of recognition, not the content of speech. Parents are not overreacting when they sense the difference between wordplay and word-erosion: one plays WITH meaning, the other practices life WITHOUT it.

The redeemable instinct. Underneath the noise is something God made: the joy of shared language, the delight of belonging marked by a password. Scripture is full of in-group words — Shibboleth, Maranatha, the new name known only to its receiver. The answer to a password of nothing is not silence but a better password: households and churches that give the young a rich, weighty, common tongue — catechism answers, psalms, the old words — so that belonging attaches to meaning instead of replacing it.
roots_summary: From Skrilla's rap Doot Doot (6 7) (2024) through basketball edits to global classroom catchphrase (2025): a proudly meaningless in-group signal, performed with a juggling gesture.
roots_lines: Skrilla, Doot Doot (6 7) — the source hook (2024)
Spread via basketball highlight edits (notably LaMelo Ball memes)
Adopted by Gen Alpha classrooms worldwide through 2025
Performed with a two-handed, palms-up juggling gesture
Named a 2025 word of the year precisely for meaning nothing
usage: Teacher: "Turn to page sixty-seven." The class, in unison: "SIX SEVEN!"
It is the laugh of belonging, not a message; the danger is a diet of belonging without meaning.
Answer a password of nothing with a better password: give your kids old words with weight.

etymology: A 2024-25 streamer-culture coinage: a softened, plural-collective mutation of a crude word for promiscuous women ("hoes" → "the huzz"), popularized by short-form clips; spawned variants like bruzz (the bros).
biblical_def: Huzz is current youth slang for girls or young women considered collectively — typically as romantic prospects: "chasing the huzz," "bring the huzz." Its cheerful sound disguises its parentage: it is a phonetic softening of a degrading word for promiscuous women, laundered through streamer culture until middle-schoolers repeat it without knowing what they are saying. That laundering is precisely what parents should decode: the word packages young women as an undifferentiated commodity-class to be pursued, counted, and joked about. The Christian observation: Scripture will not allow men to speak of women as a herd. Every one of "the huzz" is a particular image-bearer of God (Gen 1:27), somebody's daughter and somebody's sister; and the apostle's instruction to young men is exact — treat "the younger as sisters, with all purity" (1 Tim 5:2). A young man's vocabulary for women is a confession of his theology of women, and it audits his heart long before his behavior follows: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh (Matt 12:34). This one is not redeemable by softening; it is to be dropped, and replaced with the dignity of names.
webster_summary: Streamer-era collective for girls/young women ("the huzz"), a laundered mutation of a degrading term; packages image-bearers as a commodity-class — verdict: reject, and recover 1 Tim 5:2.
webster_full: HUZZ, n. collect. (Gen-Z / Gen Alpha slang, c. 2024–present) Girls or young women considered collectively, usually as romantic prospects: "chasing the huzz."
A phonetic softening of a crude word for promiscuous women, laundered by streamer culture.
Variants: bruzz (the bros), gruzz and other jocular mutations.
Many young users repeat it without knowing its parentage — which is the decode parents need.
Spoken cheerfully; degrading by design: women as a pursued herd rather than persons.
scriptures: Gen 1:27
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
1 Tim 5:2
The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity.
Matt 12:34
...out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.
Eph 4:29
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
corruption_summary: A degrading word laundered into cuteness: women packaged as a collective commodity for pursuit. The softened sound does not soften the theology; vocabulary for women is a confession of one's doctrine of the image of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Laundering by mutation. The path from the crude original to huzz is a case study in how youth dialect launders degradation: mutate the sound, keep the meaning, and the word passes school filters and parental ears while carrying the same freight — women as a class of targets. The mutation is not innocence; it is camouflage. Naming the parentage out loud usually does more than forbidding the word: most boys are embarrassed to learn what they have been saying.

The audit of the tongue. A young man who speaks of "the huzz" is rehearsing a posture toward women that will one day cost him — and them — dearly. The biblical alternative is not prudish silence about attraction but a different grammar altogether: women as mothers and sisters to be honored (1 Tim 5:2), a wife as a good thing found (Prov 18:22), and speech that ministers grace to the hearers (Eph 4:29). Fathers: give your sons the grammar of honor before the algorithm gives them the grammar of the herd.
roots_summary: Crude term for promiscuous women → phonetic softening in streamer culture (2024-25) → cheerful-sounding collective for girls ("the huzz"), with variants like bruzz.
roots_lines: Origin: a degrading English slang word for promiscuous women
Streamer culture mutates the vowel: "the huzz" (c. 2024)
Short-form clips spread it to middle-school vocabulary by 2025
Jocular variants follow: bruzz (bros), gruzz, etc.
The softened sound launders, but does not change, the meaning
usage: "He's not coming — he's out chasing the huzz." Translation: he treats girls as a herd to pursue.
Most boys are embarrassed to learn the word's parentage; tell them, and give them 1 Tim 5:2 instead.
A man's vocabulary for women is a confession of his theology of women.

etymology: Gen-Z/Gen Alpha pejorative (mainstream by 2024-25): ugly, busted, badly put together — of a person's looks, an outfit, or a botched situation. Likely from "chopped and screwed" / butcher imagery: something hacked at rather than made whole.
biblical_def: Chopped is the current all-purpose put-down for appearance: a person, haircut, outfit, or effort judged ugly or badly assembled. ("He's chopped" = he is unattractive; "the fit is chopped" = the outfit fails.) It belongs to a family of looks-ranking slang — mid, built different, the looksmaxxing scoreboard — by which the young grade one another's faces and bodies in public, constantly, for laughs. The Christian observation distinguishes the uses. Applied to things — a botched parking job, a failed recipe — it is harmless comic judgment. Applied to people, it is the schoolyard's oldest sin in fresh packaging: contempt for the workmanship of God. The God who formed every frame declares each one fearfully and wonderfully made (Psa 139:14); His own evaluation system is announced at David's anointing — man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart (1 Sam 16:7); and Proverbs warns that whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker (Prov 17:5) — a principle that reaches every mockery of what a person cannot help. A generation already drowning in appearance-anxiety does not need its church-raised kids running the same scoreboard.
webster_summary: All-purpose Gen-Z pejorative for ugly/badly-assembled (a person, outfit, or effort); harmless of things, but of people it is contempt for God's workmanship dressed as humor — examine.
webster_full: CHOPPED, adj. (Gen-Z / Gen Alpha slang, c. 2024–present) Ugly; busted; badly put together — of a person's appearance, an outfit, or a botched effort.
"He's chopped" (unattractive); "that fit is chopped" (the outfit fails); "the plan was chopped" (poorly executed).
Family resemblance: mid (mediocre), cooked (done for), the looksmaxxing scoreboard.
Imagery of something hacked at rather than crafted whole.
Decode for parents: your teen is grading faces in public; ask whose workmanship is being graded.
scriptures: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
...for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
Prov 17:5
Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: and he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished.
Jas 3:9
Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God.
corruption_summary: The looks-scoreboard in one syllable: public comic contempt for appearance. Of objects, harmless; of people, it mocks the similitude of God with the same tongue that blesses Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The scoreboard culture. Chopped is not an isolated word but the pejorative pole of a whole grading economy — looksmaxxing, mewing, mogging, mid — in which the young rank faces as content. The result is documented misery: a generation measuring itself against filtered composites and calling the losers chopped. The church's answer is not a gentler scoreboard but the abolition of the scoreboard: the LORD looketh on the heart, and His regard is not curved on a grading scale.

James's mirror. The apostle's word lands squarely: with the tongue bless we God, and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God (Jas 3:9). A youth group that laughs "chopped" at a classmate on Friday and sings on Sunday is running both halves of James's contradiction. Teach the young the joke they are actually making: every "chopped" face was composed on purpose by the Artist they claim to worship.
roots_summary: Butcher/"chopped-and-screwed" imagery → Gen-Z pejorative for ugly or badly assembled (mainstream 2024-25); the put-down pole of the looks-grading economy.
roots_lines: Imagery: hacked at, butchered — the opposite of crafted whole
Hip-hop "chopped and screwed" remix culture supplies the sound
Gen-Z adopts it as the all-purpose ugly/busted verdict (c. 2024)
Applied to faces, outfits, and failed efforts alike
Pejorative pole of the looksmaxxing/mid grading economy
usage: "Bro called MY fit chopped?" — the scoreboard always turns on its players.
Of a parking job, comedy; of a face, contempt for the Maker's workmanship (Prov 17:5).
The gospel abolishes the looks-scoreboard: the LORD looketh on the heart (1 Sam 16:7).

etymology: Clipping of opposition (or opponent), from Chicago drill rap (early 2010s), where it named rival-gang members; generalized through the 2020s to mean any enemy, hater, or rival — "watch out for the opps."
biblical_def: An opp is an enemy. In its drill-rap homeland the word was deadly literal — rival-gang members tracked and named in songs; as it generalized through gaming and school culture it came to mean anyone perceived as against you: the kid who screenshots your messages, the coworker angling for your spot, the hater in the comments. "Opps" thinking carries a whole posture: assume surveillance, assume malice, keep score, trust no one outside the circle. The Christian observation takes the word more seriously than its users do. First, Scripture agrees that the believer HAS enemies — it is not paranoia but sober doctrine: your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about (1 Pet 5:8), and the world is not neutral toward Christ's people. But Scripture assigns the enemies differently: the real opps are the world, the flesh, and the devil — not the image-bearer across the cafeteria. Toward human adversaries the Lord's command is the most counter-cultural sentence ever spoken: Love your enemies, bless them that curse you (Matt 5:44). A generation trained to sort peers into allies and opps is being discipled into tribal paranoia; the disciple instead watches the true adversary and prays for the human one.
webster_summary: Drill-rap clipping of "opposition": an enemy or hater; generalized to anyone against you. Scripture relocates the enmity — the real adversary is the devil (1 Pet 5:8); the human "opp" is to be loved and prayed for (Matt 5:44).
webster_full: OPP, n. (Gen-Z slang; Chicago drill origin, early 2010s) An enemy, rival, or hater; originally a rival-gang member, now anyone perceived as against you.
"Watch the opps" — assume surveillance and malice from outsiders.
Carries a posture: keep score, trust only the circle, read neutrality as hostility.
Generalized through gaming, sports, and school culture in the 2020s.
Decode for parents: your teen has a working doctrine of enemies; Scripture has a better one.
scriptures: Matt 5:44
But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;
1 Pet 5:8
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
Eph 6:12
For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.
Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head.
corruption_summary: Opps-culture trains tribal paranoia: every outsider a presumed enemy, every slight a war. Scripture is more realistic about enemies and more radical about their treatment — the true adversary is spiritual; the human one is to be loved.
corruption_paragraphs: Paranoia as a lifestyle. Opps-thinking assumes a world of total surveillance and zero good faith — a posture forged in actual gang war and now marketed to thirteen-year-olds as ordinary social software. It manufactures the enemies it fears: treat every peer as a potential opp and you will surely acquire some. The proverb knew the mechanism: a man that hath friends must shew himself friendly. Suspicion is not discernment; it is fear wearing discernment's jacket.

The relocated war. The gospel does not tell the young man there is no war; it tells him where the war is. We wrestle not against flesh and blood (Eph 6:12) — the cafeteria rival is not the enemy; the lion walking about is. And toward the human adversary, Christ issues commands no drill track could conceive: love, bless, do good, pray, feed (Matt 5:44; Rom 12:20). The man who obeys them is not soft; he has simply identified the real opp and refuses to do its recruiting.
roots_summary: Clipping of opposition; Chicago drill (early 2010s) for rival-gang members → generalized 2020s slang for any enemy or hater; carries a posture of tribal suspicion.
roots_lines: Clipping of opposition / opponent
Chicago drill rap, early 2010s: rival-gang members
Spreads through hip-hop, gaming, and school culture in the 2020s
Generalizes to any hater, rival, or presumed enemy
"Watch the opps": a working doctrine of enemies in two words
usage: "Can't post that — the opps will see it." A thirteen-year-old's counter-intelligence doctrine.
Scripture is more realistic: you do have an adversary, and he is not in your group chat (1 Pet 5:8).
The disciple watches the lion and feeds the rival (Rom 12:20).

etymology: Blend of situation + relationship (popularized late 2010s-2020s): a romantic and often physical involvement deliberately kept undefined — more than friends, less than committed, with the question "what are we?" permanently unasked or unanswered.
biblical_def: A situationship is a romance engineered to avoid definition: two people functioning as a couple — time, affection, often the body — while refusing the question of commitment. The form is new in name only; what is new is its institutionalization as a normal, even preferred, stage. Its appeal is honest enough to name: all of intimacy's privileges with none of covenant's obligations, and a permanent exit kept propped open. Its cost is just as nameable, and an entire generation is documenting it: chronic anxiety, asymmetric attachment (one party always quietly hopes), and years consumed in deliberate ambiguity. The Christian observation: Scripture's grammar for romance is covenant — definition is not the enemy of love but its spine. God's pattern is leave, cleave, one flesh (Gen 2:24): public, defined, sworn. The Lord's speech-ethic applies directly to the "what are we?" question: let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay (Matt 5:37) — ambiguity maintained for advantage is a form of falsehood. And the gospel exposes the deepest problem: Christ does not keep His bride in a situationship; He covenants, names, and stays. A man who wants the privileges of a wife without the vows is not in a gray area; he is withholding the one thing love is.
webster_summary: Romance deliberately kept undefined — intimacy's privileges without covenant's obligations. Scripture's grammar for love is definition: leave, cleave, one flesh (Gen 2:24); yea be yea (Matt 5:37). Verdict: reject the form, rescue the people in it.
webster_full: SITUATIONSHIP, n. (Gen-Z / Millennial slang, late 2010s–present) A romantic/physical involvement deliberately kept undefined; more than friends, less than committed.
Defining feature: the question "what are we?" is permanently unasked or deflected.
Appeal: intimacy without obligation, exit always propped open.
Documented cost: chronic ambiguity-anxiety and asymmetric hope.
Decode for parents: not a phase of courtship but the engineered avoidance of it.
scriptures: Gen 2:24
Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
Matt 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Prov 18:22
Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the LORD.
Song 8:4
I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please.
corruption_summary: The institutionalization of covenant-refusal: intimacy harvested while definition is withheld. Love's spine is definition; ambiguity maintained for advantage is falsehood with a cute name.
corruption_paragraphs: The economics of ambiguity. A situationship is rarely symmetrical: one party enjoys the option-value of the open exit while the other pays the interest in hope deferred — and Scripture has a line for that ledger: hope deferred maketh the heart sick (Prov 13:12). The refusal to define is not neutrality; it is a decision repeated daily, in favor of the party who benefits from the fog. Calling it a "situationship" launders a withholding of love into a lifestyle category.

Covenant as kindness. The biblical alternative is not instant marriage but honest definition at every stage: intentions spoken, timelines real, the body reserved for the covenant (Heb 13:4), and a yea that means yea. Definition is kindness — it lets both souls know what they may hope. The gospel pattern stands over it all: Christ loved the church and gave himself for it — named her, covenanted with her, and will not leave. Men learn to love like that, or they learn the fog; there is no third school.
roots_summary: Blend of situation + relationship (late 2010s): romance engineered to stay undefined — intimacy without covenant; rejected by Scripture's grammar of leave, cleave, one flesh.
roots_lines: Blend: situation + relationship
Popularized late 2010s-2020s as dating-app culture's resting state
Defining feature: the permanently deflected "what are we?"
Appeal: privileges of intimacy, obligations of none
Biblical contrast: covenant — public, defined, sworn (Gen 2:24)
usage: "We're not together-together — it's a situationship." Translation: one of us prefers the fog.
Definition is not the enemy of love but its spine; ambiguity kept for advantage is falsehood (Matt 5:37).
Christ does not situationship His bride: He covenants, names, and stays (Eph 5:25).

etymology: From social-media metrics (c. 2017, mainstream 2020s): a reply that earns more likes than the post it answers has "ratioed" it — the crowd's arithmetic declaring the original wrong. "L + ratio" became the all-purpose dismissal.
biblical_def: To ratio someone is to defeat them by arithmetic: when a reply gathers more likes than the post it rebuts, the crowd has voted, and the original is declared wrong — no argument required. "L + ratio" says it in four characters: you lost, and the numbers prove it. The mechanism deserves a longer look than the joke gets, because it is a complete epistemology in miniature: truth is whatever the visible majority applauds in the next twenty minutes. The Christian observation: Scripture confronted this exact arithmetic at Sinai's foot and Pilate's balcony, and legislated against it in so many words — Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil (Exo 23:2). The crowd's count is real data about the crowd; it is no data about the truth. Elijah was ratioed eight hundred fifty to one on Carmel and the fire fell on his altar (1 Kgs 18); the apostles were outvoted in every city they entered; and the broad way has always had the better numbers (Matt 7:13-14). A generation that learns to measure claims by likes is being catechized into vox populi vox Dei — the one creed the prophets uniformly died refusing. The believer takes his Ls from Scripture, not from the scoreboard.
webster_summary: Social-media defeat-by-arithmetic: a reply out-liked is a claim "disproven." A complete false epistemology in miniature — Exo 23:2 forbids following a multitude; Elijah was ratioed 850-to-1 and the fire still fell.
webster_full: RATIO, n./v. (Gen-Z social-media slang, c. 2017–present) To defeat a post by out-liking it with a reply; the unfavorable like-ratio itself.
"L + ratio" — the all-purpose dismissal: you lost, and the numbers prove it.
Mechanism: crowd applause within minutes stands in for argument.
An epistemology in miniature: the visible majority's reaction = the verdict.
Decode for parents: your teen's generation is being trained to let the scoreboard settle truth.
scriptures: Exo 23:2
Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil; neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment:
Matt 7:13
Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat:
Gal 1:10
For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
Then said Elijah unto the people, I, even I only, remain a prophet of the LORD; but Baal's prophets are four hundred and fifty men.
corruption_summary: Truth-by-headcount, gamified: the like-ratio as verdict. Scripture's entire prophetic history is a polemic against deciding truth by the multitude's applause.
corruption_paragraphs: The twenty-minute majority. The ratio does not even measure the multitude; it measures the fraction of the multitude that happened to scroll past in the first minutes, pre-sorted by an algorithm that profits from pile-ons. It is mob justice with a scoreboard — and like all mobs it is a coward's court: no cross-examination, no evidence, no appeal. Teaching the young to read a like-count as a verdict is teaching them to outsource conscience to whoever assembles fastest.

The prophet's arithmetic. The Bible's heroes are, almost without exception, men who lost the ratio: Noah against the world, Micaiah against four hundred court prophets, Elijah alone on Carmel, the Lord Himself against the crowd crying Crucify. The fire fell on the outnumbered altar. The church must say it plainly to its young: the broad way always trends; do not follow a multitude to do evil, and do not mistake an L from the crowd for an L from God.
roots_summary: Social-media metric (c. 2017): a reply out-liking its target "ratioes" it — defeat by crowd arithmetic; rejected by Exo 23:2 and the whole prophetic record of righteous men who lost the count.
roots_lines: Social-media metrics: replies vs. likes as a visible scoreboard

Algorithmic pile-ons pre-sort the "majority" that votes
Biblical contrast: Elijah ratioed 850-to-1, and the fire fell (1 Kgs 18)

etymology: Deliberate respelling of tough (with hip-hop lineage back through decades of "tuff" in titles and graffiti); in 2024-25 youth usage it means cool, hard, impressive in style — "that fit is tuff," "tuff jersey."
biblical_def: Tuff is approval-slang: cool with a connotation of hardness — an outfit, car, jersey, or moment that looks impressively strong. The respelling is the point: tough describes endurance; tuff awards style. It is, on its face, one of the more innocent items in the current dialect — a compliment, cousin to fire and clean, and a father can receive "that truck is tuff" as the gift it is. The Christian observation is therefore gentle but real: notice what a culture's compliments crown. Tuff admires the look of strength — the silhouette, the posture, the aesthetic of hardness — and a steady diet of admiring strength's look can quietly teach that the look is the thing. Scripture enjoys real strength (the LORD is a man of war; the Proverbs praise the lion-bold righteous) but pointedly refuses to be impressed by its appearance: He delighteth not in the strength of the horse... the LORD taketh pleasure in them that fear him (Psa 147:10-11), and the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God (2 Cor 10:4). Receive the compliment; aim the admiration: the tuffest thing a young man will ever see is a meek man who cannot be moved.
webster_summary: Approval-slang: cool-with-hardness ("that fit is tuff"). Innocent as compliments go — but note what the culture's compliments crown: the look of strength. God delights not in the horse's strength (Psa 147:10-11). Verdict: neutral.
webster_full: TUFF, adj. (Gen-Z / Gen Alpha slang, c. 2024–present) Cool, hard, impressively styled: "that jersey is tuff."
Deliberate respelling of tough: endurance respelled as aesthetics.
Cousin compliments: fire, clean, hard, goes hard.
Long hip-hop and graffiti lineage of the "tuff" spelling.
Decode for parents: a genuine compliment — receive it, then aim the admiration at real strength.
scriptures: He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man.
The LORD taketh pleasure in them that fear him, in those that hope in his mercy.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
Prov 16:32
He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
corruption_summary: Largely innocent approval-slang; the only watch-item is what it crowns — the aesthetic of hardness — in a culture that already confuses the look of strength with the thing itself.
corruption_paragraphs: The look versus the load. Tough is proven under load; tuff is awarded on sight. The respelling accidentally documents a cultural drift: strength as costume. The young man who curates a tuff exterior can remain unsupplied for any actual weight — and the first real load finds him out. Proverbs grades the other way: he that ruleth his spirit is better than he that taketh a city (Prov 16:32) — the tuffest men in the room are usually the quietest about it.

This entry is largely innocent; the principle to aim is admiration. Compliments are a catechism in miniature — they teach the young what is worth wanting. Receive "tuff" as the gift it is, then enlarge it: show them David refusing Saul's armor, Daniel serene in the lions' den, Christ silent before Pilate — strength that never needed the silhouette. The LORD taketh pleasure in them that fear him; teach them to want THAT compliment.
roots_summary: Respelling of tough with hip-hop/graffiti lineage; 2024-25 youth approval-slang for cool-with-hardness — endurance respelled as aesthetics; neutral, with admiration worth aiming.

etymology: Clipping of uncle (AAVE roots as a respectful-familiar address for an older man); 2024-25 youth usage flips it playful-mocking: an "unc" is a man aging out of youth culture — "unc status" begins, by their clock, around thirty.
biblical_def: Unc is what the young now call a man who is no longer one of them: the thirty-something at the pickup game, the teacher who says "lit," the older brother's friend. Rooted in the genuinely warm use of uncle as respectful address, the current usage runs both directions at once — affection and gentle mockery: "unc still got it" (admiring) or "rest up, unc" (you are old; sit down). The Christian observation enjoys the warmth and corrects the clock. The warmth: a culture reaching for kinship words for non-kin elders is groping toward something biblical — the apostle tells Timothy to treat "the elder men as fathers" (1 Tim 5:1), and a church full of uncs in that sense is healthy. The clock: a dialect that retires men at thirty has its honor-curve exactly inverted. Scripture commands the young to rise before the hoary head (Lev 19:32) and crowns age found in righteousness as glory (Prov 16:31); the beauty of young men may be their strength, but the splendor belongs to the gray (Prov 20:29). Take the nickname with a grin — then let the unc do what uncs are biblically FOR: teach, charge, and disciple the very youths who named him (Titus 2:2, 6).
webster_summary: Playful-mocking clipping of "uncle" for a man aging out of youth culture ("unc status"). The kinship instinct is biblical (1 Tim 5:1); the retirement-at-thirty clock is inverted (Lev 19:32; Prov 20:29). Verdict: examine — then go be a Titus-2 unc.
webster_full: UNC, n. (Gen-Z / Gen Alpha slang, c. 2024–present) An older man relative to youth culture; affectionate and/or gently mocking: "unc still got it."
From the warm AAVE address unc/uncle for a respected older man.
"Unc status": by the dialect's clock, begins around thirty.
Both directions at once: kinship-honor and you're-old mockery.
Decode for parents: you have been drafted as an elder; Scripture has a job description for that (Titus 2).
scriptures: Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD.
Prov 20:29
The glory of young men is their strength: and the beauty of old men is the gray head.
1 Tim 5:1
Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father; and the younger men as brethren;
Titus 2:2
That the aged men be sober, grave, temperate, sound in faith, in charity, in patience.
corruption_summary: Half-warm, half-inverted: the kinship address is biblical instinct; the retirement-at-thirty honor-curve is the age-despising spirit Scripture flatly reverses.
corruption_paragraphs: The inverted honor-curve. A culture that pensions men off at thirty has confused currency with worth: a man's value tracks his fluency in this season's dialect, so the gray head — which Scripture crowns — reads as expiration. Rehoboam ran that experiment, despising the old men's counsel for his age-mates', and split a kingdom (1 Kgs 12). The young who mock unc-status are sawing at the branch they will sit on sooner than they think — unc status comes for every man who lives.

The drafted elder. The redeemable half is better than the joke knows: the young are instinctively assigning kinship roles to non-kin men, which is exactly the church's design — elder men as fathers, aged men sober and sound, teaching the young (1 Tim 5:1; Titus 2:2-6). So take the nickname and execute the office: an unc who shows up, keeps his word, opens his Bible, and charges young men like a father is not aging out of the culture; he is what the culture is starving for.
roots_summary: Clipping of uncle (warm AAVE address for an older man) → 2024-25 playful-mocking title for men aging out of youth culture; the kinship instinct is biblical, the honor-curve inverted.

etymology: New York slang (decades old locally; nationalized by social media in the late 2010s-2020s): "completely serious" — an emphasis-oath certifying that the speaker is not joking: "I'm deadass," "deadass the best slice in Brooklyn."
biblical_def: Deadass is a sincerity-certificate: dropped before or after a claim, it swears the speaker is completely serious. ("Deadass?" / "Deadass." is an entire verified exchange.) Parents should hear two things in it. First, the obvious: it carries a coarse fragment, and a tongue trained toward grace finds cleaner tools (Eph 4:29; Col 4:6). Second, the subtler and more interesting thing: the word exists because ordinary speech has stopped being believed. A generation marinated in irony, exaggeration, and engagement-bait must now NOTARIZE its sentences — deadass, no cap, fr fr, on God — a whole stack of mini-oaths to purchase what a plain word once carried. The Lord's teaching lands on this stack with precision: let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil (Matt 5:37). The escalation of oaths is the inflation of a devalued currency — and the devaluation is the real story. The Christian alternative is not a holier intensifier but a reputation: a man whose plain yes has never needed a notary. Let him say a thing once, unadorned, and be believed — that is the quiet glory the whole deadass economy is bankrupt for.
webster_summary: NYC sincerity-oath ("completely serious"), nationalized by social media; one of the stack of mini-oaths (no cap, on God, fr fr) a low-trust speech economy now requires. Matt 5:37: the plain yea needs no notary. Verdict: examine.
webster_full: DEADASS, adv./adj. (NYC slang, nationalized late 2010s–present) Completely serious; not joking: "I'm deadass."
"Deadass?" / "Deadass." functions as a complete claim-and-verification exchange.
Belongs to the sincerity-oath stack: no cap, on God, fr fr, I swear.
Carries a coarse fragment; cleaner tools exist for a tongue trained toward grace.
Decode for parents: the word exists because plain speech stopped being believed — that is the story.
scriptures: Matt 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Jas 5:12
But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.
Eph 4:29
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
Col 4:6
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
corruption_summary: A sincerity-oath for a low-trust speech economy: when every sentence performs, plain words need notarizing. The oath-stack is inflation; the cure is a yes that has never lied.
corruption_paragraphs: The trust deficit. Deadass, no cap, on God, fr fr — the young carry more oath-instruments than a medieval court, and for the same reason courts needed them: the default assumption is exaggeration. Christ's teaching in Matt 5 was aimed at exactly such a stack (by heaven, by the earth, by Jerusalem, by thy head) — graded oaths that let speech be mostly worthless and occasionally guaranteed. His remedy was not a better oath but the abolition of the tiers: ALL your words should be the reliable kind.

The coarse fragment and the cleaner tongue. The word's tail is crude, and Christians need not pretend otherwise: out of the same mouth ought not proceed blessing and coarseness (Eph 4:29; Jas 3:10). But the deeper discipleship issue is the economy it serves. Raise young people whose plain sentences are collateralized by their character — whose yes has simply never bounced — and the entire notarizing apparatus becomes unnecessary in their mouths. That is not prudishness; it is wealth.
roots_summary: NYC slang for "completely serious," nationalized by social media; one mini-oath in the sincerity stack (no cap, on God, fr fr) that a low-trust, irony-saturated speech economy now requires.
